questions.question: Estimate the length of the neck of the adult giraffe from the shoulders, using the information in the photograph.
questions.answer: About 1.9 m (accept about 1.8 to 2.0 m).
steps: Scale: the arrow from the ground to the dashed shoulder line stands for 3.0 m.
Measure the neck from the shoulders to the top of the head: it is about 0.65 times the length of the 3.0 m arrow.
Neck length = 0.65 x 3.0 m = about 1.9 m.
Any sensible estimate obtained by measuring the photograph and scaling against the 3.0 m arrow is acceptable.

questions.question: Explain why the heart of a giraffe, which can be 60 cm long, needs to be so large.
questions.answer: The heart must generate very high blood pressure to pump blood up the long neck against gravity to the brain.
steps: The giraffe's head is several metres above the heart, so blood must be pumped against gravity.
A large, thick-walled ventricle generates the high pressure needed to push blood up the neck.
Blood must reach the brain at a pressure high enough to keep it supplied with oxygen and glucose.
A large heart also gives a large stroke volume, so enough blood reaches the brain and other tissues each beat.

questions.question: Draw a labelled diagram of an artery as seen in section.
questions.answer: A thick wall with a narrow-ish lumen, showing endothelium, elastic tissue, smooth muscle and a collagen-rich outer layer; labels for the lumen and layers.
steps: Draw a circle for the artery with a small, round lumen at the centre.
Draw a thin inner layer of endothelium lining the lumen, with folded elastic tissue beneath it.
Draw a thick middle layer of smooth muscle and elastic fibres, which is much thicker than in a vein.
Draw an outer layer of collagen and connective tissue, then label the lumen, endothelium, elastic layer and smooth muscle.

questions.question: Explain why the arteries near the heart of a giraffe are highly elastic.
questions.answer: The elastic walls stretch to take the high pressure surge from each heartbeat and then recoil, maintaining pressure and smoothing blood flow.
steps: Each ventricular contraction forces a surge of blood into the arteries at high pressure.
Elastic fibres in the arterial wall stretch to accommodate this surge, storing energy.
Elastic recoil keeps blood flowing steadily to the tissues between heartbeats.
During diastole the elastic walls recoil, pushing blood forward and keeping the pressure high between beats.

questions.question: Explain why very narrow capillaries near the skin surface prevent excessive bleeding if the legs are damaged.
questions.answer: Narrow capillaries give high resistance and low blood pressure, so blood flows out of a damaged vessel slowly and clotting can seal it.
steps: Narrow vessels create a high resistance to blood flow.
This keeps the blood pressure in the capillaries low.
Narrow vessels also slow the flow, so clotting has more time to seal the wound.
Low pressure means blood leaks out of a damaged capillary slowly, giving time for clotting to seal the wound.

questions.topic: Small Red Cells and Oxygen Supply
questions.question: Explain why smaller red blood cells, about one third the size of human cells, increase the supply of oxygen to the legs.
questions.answer: Smaller cells have a larger surface area to volume ratio and a shorter diffusion distance, and more cells can pass through capillaries, so oxygen is released faster.
steps: Smaller red blood cells have a larger surface area to volume ratio than larger cells.
A larger ratio means oxygen can diffuse out of the cell and into the tissues faster.
Their small size lets them pass through very narrow capillaries, so they reach the tissues in the legs.
More cells can therefore pass per unit time, increasing the total oxygen delivered.

questions.question: From a table of features of transport mechanisms, identify the feature that is true for active transport only, facilitated diffusion only, both, or neither.
questions.answer: Passive process: facilitated diffusion only. Membrane proteins involved: both active transport and facilitated diffusion. Can be up the concentration gradient: active transport only.
steps: Passive process: facilitated diffusion needs no ATP and goes down the gradient, whereas active transport needs ATP, so tick "facilitated diffusion only".
Membrane proteins: facilitated diffusion uses channel or carrier proteins and active transport uses carrier proteins (pumps), so tick "both".
Direction: only active transport can move a substance up (against) its concentration gradient, so tick "active transport only".

questions.topic: Uptake of Substances K and L
questions.question: Explain the differences in the uptake of substance K and substance L into an amoeba at 18 C, shown on the graph.
questions.answer: K is taken up at a steady rate that carries on for the whole 5 hours, whereas L is taken up more slowly and levels off at about 11.5 ug cm-3 after about 3.8 hours.
steps: K rises steadily from about 0.7 to about 18.5 ug cm-3 (about 3.6 ug cm-3 per hour) with no levelling off, so its uptake is not stopped by the gradient disappearing: it is active transport using ATP, moving K up its concentration gradient.
L rises more slowly (about 2.5 ug cm-3 per hour, starting at about 2 ug cm-3), then stays flat at about 11.5 ug cm-3 from about 3.8 hours.

The plateau for L means no net uptake: it moves passively (facilitated diffusion) down its gradient, so uptake stops once the concentration in the cytoplasm equals that outside, or when all the carrier/channel proteins are saturated.
So K needs energy and can keep accumulating, whereas L is passive and limited by the gradient or the number of transport proteins.

questions.question: On the graph, draw a line to show the uptake of substance L at 10 C.
questions.answer: A straight line starting at about 2 ug cm-3 at 0 hours, with a smaller gradient than the 18 C line for L, so it lies below it and reaches any plateau later (it may still be rising at 5 hours).
steps: At 10 C the molecules and carrier proteins have less kinetic energy and the membrane is less fluid, so uptake is slower than at 18 C.
Start the line at the same point as the 18 C line (about 2 ug cm-3 at 0 hours) because nothing has happened yet.
Draw a straight line with a shallower slope than the 18 C line (less than about 2.5 ug cm-3 per hour, for example reaching about 8 to 9 ug cm-3 at 3.8 hours).
Any plateau should occur later than 3.8 hours and, if equilibrium sets the limit, at the same concentration of about 11.5 ug cm-3.

questions.question: Explain why the cell surface membrane is able to change its shape when cytoplasm flows towards it to form pseudopodia.
questions.answer: The phospholipids in the membrane can move past one another, so the fluid bilayer deforms and the membrane changes shape.
steps: The cell surface membrane is a phospholipid bilayer that is fluid, not rigid.
Phospholipid molecules can move laterally past each other, so the membrane flows.
The cytoskeleton (actin filaments) pushes and reorganises the membrane at each pseudopodium.
Proteins and cholesterol are embedded in this fluid mosaic, allowing it to stretch and deform as cytoplasm pushes against it.

questions.question: Explain how the uptake of substances would be affected if the amoeba increased its number of pseudopodia.
questions.answer: More pseudopodia increase the membrane surface area available for endocytosis and phagocytosis, so more substances are taken in per unit time.
steps: Pseudopodia surround food and water, forming vesicles by endocytosis.
Each extra pseudopodium adds membrane surface area for engulfing substances.
A larger surface area allows more vesicles to form in a given time.
So the overall rate of uptake of substances increases.

questions.question: Calculate the volume of the liposome shown in the diagram, using the formula given in the question.
steps: The 100 nm arrow is the diameter, so r = 100 / 2 = 50 nm.
V = 523 599 nm^3 = 5.2 x 10^5 nm^3 (2 s.f.); the unit is nm^3.

questions.question: Explain the arrangement of phospholipids in liposomes made by adding phospholipids to water.
questions.answer: Hydrophilic heads face the water on the outside and inside, while hydrophobic tails point inwards, away from water, forming a bilayer sphere.
steps: Phospholipids have a hydrophilic phosphate head and two hydrophobic fatty acid tails.
In water the heads are attracted to the water and face outwards, both on the outer and inner surfaces.
The hydrophobic tails are shielded from the water and point towards the centre of the membrane.
This forms a spherical phospholipid bilayer, the liposome.

questions.question: How does glycerol pass through the liposome membrane? Options: A active transport, B diffusion, C endocytosis, D osmosis.
questions.answer: B (diffusion).
steps: Glycerol is a small molecule that moves down its concentration gradient.
No ATP is used and no vesicles form, so it is not active transport or endocytosis.
Its movement depends only on the concentration gradient across the liposome membrane.
Osmosis refers only to the movement of water, so D is wrong; the answer is simple diffusion.

questions.question: Describe the effects of cholesterol and temperature on membrane permeability to glycerol, as shown in the graph.
questions.answer: Permeability to glycerol increases as temperature rises in all three liposomes, and at any temperature it decreases as the proportion of cholesterol increases.
steps: Temperature: permeability rises with temperature for every liposome, and the curves get steeper at higher temperature; with no cholesterol it rises from about 10 a.u. at 1 C to about 280 a.u. at 30 C.
Cholesterol: at each temperature the permeability is highest with no cholesterol, lower with 20% and lowest with 50% cholesterol; at 30 C it is about 280, 155 and 85 a.u. respectively.
At 20 C the values are about 150, 75 and 25 a.u., so 50% cholesterol cuts the permeability to about a sixth.
With 50% cholesterol the permeability is about zero below about 13 C, and its curve is the flattest, so cholesterol also reduces the effect of temperature.

questions.topic: Why Cholesterol and Temperature Affect Permeability
questions.question: Explain why cholesterol and temperature affect membrane permeability.
questions.answer: Cholesterol packs between phospholipids and reduces fluidity, lowering permeability; higher temperature increases kinetic energy and fluidity, raising permeability.
steps: Cholesterol sits between the phospholipid tails and restricts their movement.
This makes the membrane less fluid and less permeable to small molecules such as glycerol.
Higher temperature gives phospholipids more kinetic energy, so they move more and the membrane becomes more fluid.
A more fluid membrane allows more glycerol to diffuse through, increasing permeability.

questions.question: The mouse is 3 cm tall. Using the white line on the elephant photograph, calculate how many times taller the elephant is than the mouse.
questions.answer: About 80 times taller (about 82).
steps: Measure the white line on the elephant photograph: it is about 4.9 cm long.
Actual height = image size / magnification = 4.9 / 0.02 = about 245 cm.
Ratio = 245 cm / 3 cm = about 82, so the elephant is about 80 times taller than the mouse.
The exact value depends on the measured length (a 5.0 cm line gives 250 cm and a ratio of 83).

questions.question: The lungs of an elephant are attached to the chest wall and diaphragm by collagen fibres. Describe how the lungs are adapted for gas exchange.
questions.answer: The attachments keep the lungs expanded so alveoli stay open, giving a large surface area and efficient gas exchange across thin, well-supplied walls.
steps: Collagen fibres attach the lungs to the chest wall and diaphragm, so the lungs are held open.
This stops the alveoli from collapsing, keeping a large surface area for gas exchange.
The alveolar walls are thin, giving a short diffusion distance for oxygen and carbon dioxide.
A rich capillary network around the alveoli maintains a steep concentration gradient.

questions.question: Explain the difference in the oxygen dissociation curves of haemoglobin for a mouse and an elephant, using both graphs.
questions.answer: The mouse haemoglobin has a lower affinity for oxygen (its curve is to the right) than the elephant haemoglobin, because the mouse has a much higher mass-specific metabolic rate and needs oxygen unloaded more readily to its tissues.
steps: Graph 1: at the same partial pressure of oxygen the elephant haemoglobin is more saturated (for example about 75-80% against about 30% at 4 kPa), so the elephant curve lies to the left and has the higher affinity.
Graph 2: the mouse has a mass-specific metabolic rate of about 5 cm3 oxygen g-1 hr-1 compared with about 0.2 for the elephant, so its tissues use about 25 times more oxygen per gram.

The mouse therefore needs a haemoglobin that releases (unloads) oxygen readily at the tissues, even at fairly high partial pressures; a lower affinity does this, and it still loads fully in the lungs at high partial pressure.
The elephant respires much more slowly per gram, so it needs less oxygen delivered per gram and its higher-affinity haemoglobin loads easily and unloads less readily.
The mouse has a large surface area to volume ratio and loses heat quickly, which explains its high metabolic rate.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the structure of a triglyceride and a phospholipid.
questions.answer: Both have a glycerol backbone joined to fatty acids by ester bonds; a triglyceride has three fatty acids, whereas a phospholipid has two fatty acids and a phosphate-containing head.
steps: Similarity: both contain a glycerol backbone with fatty acid chains attached by ester bonds.
Similarity: both are made of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen and are lipids.
Difference: a triglyceride has three fatty acid chains, all hydrophobic.
Difference: a phospholipid has two fatty acids and a phosphate group, giving a hydrophilic head and hydrophobic tails.

questions.question: Explain why the properties of LDLs enable cholesterol to be transported in the blood.
questions.answer: LDL has a surface of phospholipid and protein that is soluble in plasma, while its hydrophobic core carries cholesterol and other lipids safely through the water-based blood.
steps: Cholesterol is hydrophobic and cannot dissolve in the water-based blood plasma on its own.
LDL is a lipoprotein with a surface layer of phospholipids whose hydrophilic heads face the plasma.
The hydrophobic core of the LDL holds cholesterol and other lipids away from the water.
Apolipoproteins on the surface are recognised by receptors on cells, so cholesterol is delivered to them.

questions.question: Complete the table by calculating the volume of LDL (diameters 19 to 24 nm) and the ratio of LDL volume to cholesterol volume, using the formula given.
questions.answer: Volume of LDL = 7240 nm^3 (7238 nm^3); ratio of LDL volume to cholesterol volume = 14 : 1.
steps: Diameter 24 nm, so r = 12 nm.
Ratio = 7238 / 523 = 13.8, which is 14 : 1 (written as in the 19 nm row, 3590 / 523 = 7 : 1).

questions.question: Explain why measuring only the level of LDL in the blood is not a reliable predictor of cardiovascular disease, using the graph of LDL and HDL against risk.
questions.answer: The risk of CVD depends on the level of HDL as well as LDL: with high HDL the risk stays low even when LDL is high, whereas with low HDL the risk is higher and rises steeply with LDL, so LDL alone is not a reliable predictor.
steps: Graph: with HDL 0.65 and 1.16 a.u. the risk of CVD rises clearly as LDL rises (the 1.16 line rises steeply at high LDL), but with HDL 1.68 and 2.20 a.u. the lines are low and almost flat, so a high LDL level adds little risk.

At any given LDL the risk falls as HDL rises; even the lowest LDL with HDL 0.65 a.u. gives a higher risk than the highest LDL with HDL 2.20 a.u., so a person with high LDL and high HDL may be at lower risk than someone with moderate LDL and low HDL.

Own knowledge: LDL carries cholesterol to tissues and can deposit it in artery walls (atheroma and atherosclerosis), whereas HDL carries cholesterol away from the tissues to the liver, protecting against CVD; the HDL : LDL ratio matters.
From the question: LDLs cause damage after being absorbed by endothelial cells and broken down by free radicals, so the damage depends on other factors as well as the amount of LDL.
Other risk factors (smoking, high blood pressure, diet, genes, age, inactivity) also affect CVD, so LDL alone is only a partial predictor.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term partial pressure.
questions.answer: The pressure exerted by one gas in a mixture of gases; it is the proportion of the total pressure contributed by that gas.
steps: A gas mixture exerts a total pressure, shared between its component gases.
The partial pressure of one gas is the pressure that gas alone would exert.
It is measured in kPa, which is why the partial pressure of oxygen is quoted in kPa.
It equals the mole fraction of that gas multiplied by the total pressure.

questions.question: Explain how the structure of haemoglobin causes its oxygen dissociation curve to be sigmoidal (S-shaped).
questions.answer: Haemoglobin has four polypeptide chains with haem groups; binding one oxygen changes its shape and increases affinity for further oxygen (cooperative binding), giving the S shape.
steps: Haemoglobin has four polypeptide chains, each with a haem group that can bind one oxygen molecule.
When the first oxygen binds, the quaternary structure changes shape.
This change makes it easier for the next oxygen molecules to bind, so affinity increases.
The curve is therefore shallow at low partial pressure, steep in the middle, and levels off at saturation.

questions.question: Suggest why the partial pressure of oxygen in the alveoli is lower than in the atmosphere.
questions.answer: Oxygen diffuses from the alveoli into the blood, and the alveolar air is diluted by carbon dioxide and water vapour, so oxygen pressure is lower.
steps: Oxygen is continuously absorbed from the alveolar air into the blood by diffusion.
The alveolar air also contains carbon dioxide and water vapour, which dilute the oxygen.
Alveolar air is mixed with air left in the lungs after breathing, which dilutes the oxygen.
So the partial pressure of oxygen in the alveoli is lower than in the atmosphere.

questions.question: Explain why the partial pressure of oxygen decreases as blood flows through the arteries and into the veins.
questions.answer: Oxygen diffuses out of the blood into respiring tissues down a concentration gradient, and tissues use oxygen in respiration, so the blood oxygen pressure falls.
steps: Respiring tissue cells use oxygen for aerobic respiration, so their oxygen concentration stays low.
Oxygen diffuses from the blood into the tissues down the concentration gradient.
As oxygen leaves the blood, the partial pressure of oxygen in the blood falls.
This continues through the capillaries, so the venous blood has a lower oxygen pressure than the arterial blood.

questions.question: Using the point X on the graph and the oxygen dissociation curve, determine the percentage saturation of haemoglobin in blood leaving the lungs of the person at high altitude.
questions.answer: About 83% (accept 80 to 85%).
steps: Point X marks the partial pressure of oxygen in the alveoli at high altitude: about 6.3 kPa.
Blood leaving the lungs is in equilibrium with alveolar air, so its partial pressure of oxygen is also about 6.3 kPa.
Reading from the dissociation curve at 6.3 kPa gives a percentage saturation of about 83%.

questions.question: Explain why the percentage saturation of haemoglobin in a person at high altitude is much lower than in a person at sea level.
questions.answer: Lower partial pressure of oxygen at altitude means less oxygen loads onto haemoglobin, so the curve gives a lower percentage saturation.
steps: At high altitude the air contains less oxygen, so the partial pressure of oxygen in the alveoli is lower.
Less oxygen diffuses into the blood, so the partial pressure in the blood is lower.
On the oxygen dissociation curve, a lower partial pressure gives a lower saturation of haemoglobin.
So the blood carries less oxygen, although the body may respond with more red blood cells over time.

questions.question: Explain why water enters the paramecium, which lives in pond water.
questions.answer: The cytoplasm of the paramecium has a lower water potential than the pond water, so water enters by osmosis across the cell membrane.
steps: The cytoplasm of the paramecium contains dissolved solutes, giving it a lower water potential than the pond water.
Water moves down its water potential gradient by osmosis.
Water enters by osmosis, so its entry is passive and needs no ATP.
Water crosses the cell surface membrane by osmosis, entering the cell continuously.

questions.question: Explain the importance of the contractile vacuole in the paramecium.
questions.answer: The contractile vacuole actively pumps excess water out of the cell, using ATP, so the cell does not swell and burst.
steps: Water enters the paramecium continuously by osmosis because its cytoplasm is hypertonic.
The contractile vacuole collects this water and pumps it out of the cell.
This pumping uses ATP, because the water must be moved against the water potential gradient.
Without it, the cell would take in too much water, swell and burst (lysis).

questions.question: Explain the results of an investigation in which paramecia in pond water, solution A and solution B had the number of contractile vacuole pumps counted in 30-second intervals, using the graphs.
questions.answer: The pumping rate matches the rate at which water enters by osmosis: it stays at 2 per 30 s in pond water, falls to 1 in solution A (less water enters) and rises to 4 in solution B (more water enters).
steps: Pond water: 2 pumps per 30 s all the time, so water enters and is pumped out at a steady rate and the cell volume stays constant.

Solution A: starts at 2 but falls to 1 from 1 minute and stays at 1; A has a lower water potential (more concentrated) than pond water, so the water potential gradient into the cell is smaller, less water enters by osmosis and the vacuole needs to pump less often.

Solution B: rises from 2 at 0.5 minutes to 3 at 1 minute and 4 from 1.5 minutes; B has a higher water potential (more dilute) than pond water, so a steeper gradient means more water enters by osmosis and the vacuole must pump twice as often as in pond water.
The delay of 0.5 to 1.5 minutes before the rate changes shows the time the paramecia take to adjust before they reach a new steady rate.
Pumping water out uses ATP, so more energy is used in B than in pond water or A; the vacuole stops the cell swelling and bursting.

questions.question: From a table of sugars, identify the row that shows which sugars are monosaccharides and which are disaccharides.
questions.answer: C: fructose and glucose are the monosaccharides; sucrose only is the disaccharide.
steps: Glucose and fructose are single sugar units, so they are monosaccharides.
Sucrose is made of one glucose and one fructose joined together, so it is a disaccharide.

questions.question: Which type of bond joins two monosaccharides to form a disaccharide? Options: A ester, B glycosidic, C peptide, D phosphodiester.
questions.answer: B (glycosidic bond).
steps: Two monosaccharides are joined by a condensation reaction that removes water.
The bond formed between sugar units is a glycosidic bond.
A glycosidic bond forms between one sugar and the hydroxyl group of the other, releasing water.
Peptide bonds join amino acids, phosphodiester bonds join nucleotides, and ester bonds join fatty acids to glycerol, so B is correct.

questions.question: Calculate the mean concentration of glucose in three pineapples, giving the answer in g dm-3, using the table of sugar concentrations.
Explain what the solution of sugars should contain to preserve pineapples by osmotic dehydration, using the table of sugar concentrations.
questions.answer: The solution should contain all three sugars (fructose, glucose and sucrose) in about the same proportions as in the pineapple, but with a higher overall concentration (lower water potential) than the pineapple cells.
steps: Water must leave the pineapple by osmosis through its partially permeable membranes, so the solution needs a lower water potential (a higher total sugar concentration) than the pineapple tissue; this reduces the water content.

If a sugar were missing from the solution it would diffuse out of the pineapple down its concentration gradient, so the pineapple would lose that sugar and its taste would change; so fructose, glucose and sucrose must all be present.
Each sugar should be about the same concentration as in the pineapple (mean of about 1.5 g cm-3 fructose, 1.1 g cm-3 glucose and 8.6 g cm-3 sucrose) so there is little net diffusion of any sugar.
The proportions should stay as in the pineapple: sucrose is by far the main sugar (about 8 times glucose), with fructose slightly more than glucose (about 1.4 times).
Keeping the sugar concentrations in the pineapple unchanged keeps its sweet taste, while water loss preserves it.

questions.question: Explain how the electron micrograph of a 5.00 nm wide cell membrane provides evidence for its structure, using the head diameter (0.8 to 0.9 nm) and tail length (1.25 to 1.75 nm).
questions.answer: A bilayer of two heads and two tails has a width of 4.1 to 5.3 nm, which matches the measured 5.00 nm, supporting the phospholipid bilayer model.
steps: The micrograph shows two dark outer layers (hydrophilic phosphate heads) and a lighter central layer (hydrophobic tails).
The full membrane thickness is two heads plus two tails: 2(0.8 to 0.9) + 2(1.25 to 1.75) = 4.1 to 5.3 nm.
The measured width of 5.00 nm falls inside this range, so the measured membrane matches a phospholipid bilayer.
This is evidence for the bilayer structure with heads facing outwards and tails inwards.

questions.question: Explain the location of cholesterol in cell membranes, using the diagram of a cholesterol molecule (formula C27H46O).
questions.answer: Cholesterol sits within the phospholipid bilayer, with its hydrophobic steroid rings among the fatty acid tails and its small polar hydroxyl group near the phospholipid heads.
steps: Cholesterol has a large non-polar steroid ring structure, which is hydrophobic.
It has only one small polar hydroxyl (-OH) group, which is hydrophilic.
The steroid rings sit between the fatty acid tails of the phospholipids, while the -OH group sits near the phosphate heads.
So cholesterol is embedded within the bilayer, where it helps regulate membrane fluidity.

questions.question: Describe the dipolar nature of water.
questions.answer: Oxygen is more electronegative than hydrogen, so the shared electrons are pulled towards oxygen, giving the oxygen a partial negative charge and each hydrogen a partial positive charge.
steps: Oxygen attracts the shared electron pairs in the O-H bonds more strongly than hydrogen does.
This makes the oxygen end slightly negative (delta-) and the hydrogen ends slightly positive (delta+).
The bent shape of water means the partial charges do not cancel, making water polar.
The bent shape of the water molecule means the charges do not cancel, so water is a polar molecule with a dipole.

questions.question: Explain the permeability of cell membranes to sodium and chloride ions, glucose, water and a steroid, which are polar or non-polar.
questions.answer: Non-polar steroids pass freely through the hydrophobic core; ions and glucose cannot pass easily; water passes slowly because it is small and polar.
steps: The phospholipid bilayer has a hydrophobic core, which non-polar molecules such as steroids dissolve in and cross easily.
Ions are charged and strongly hydrated, so they cannot cross the hydrophobic core and need channel or carrier proteins.
Glucose is polar and too large to diffuse through the bilayer, so it needs a carrier protein (facilitated diffusion).
Water is small and polar, so it crosses slowly by simple diffusion, and faster through aquaporins.

questions.question: Explain how the graph shows a correlation between smoking and death rate from lung cancer in men.
questions.answer: Both the number of cigarettes smoked and the death rate rise and then fall, with the death rate following the smoking pattern about 15 years later, which is a positive correlation.
steps: Cigarettes smoked rise from 1945 to a peak at about 1980 and then fall.
The death rate from lung cancer rises from about 1960 to a peak at about 1995 and then falls, so the two curves have the same shape and move in the same direction.
The death rate lags about 15 years behind smoking, consistent with the time cancer takes to develop.
The graph shows a correlation only; it does not prove that smoking causes the deaths.

questions.question: People with emphysema have weakened alveoli that collapse, creating fewer but larger alveoli. Explain how this affects gas exchange.
questions.answer: Fewer, larger alveoli give a smaller total surface area and a lower surface area to volume ratio, so diffusion of oxygen and carbon dioxide is slower.
steps: Gas exchange happens across the alveolar walls, so the total surface area of alveoli sets the rate.
Fewer alveoli reduce the total surface area available for diffusion.
Larger alveoli have a smaller surface area to volume ratio, and diffusion distances can increase in collapsed regions.
So less oxygen enters the blood and less carbon dioxide leaves, reducing gas exchange efficiency.

questions.question: Explain the factors that determine the rate of diffusion of gases between the air and the tissues of a bird embryo, using the egg shell thickness (0.5 mm) and pore density (40 to 400 per cm2).
questions.answer: Rate depends on the number of pores (surface area for diffusion), the shell thickness (diffusion distance), the concentration gradient of gases, and temperature.
steps: Diffusion rate is proportional to the surface area available, so more pores per cm2 (up to 400) allow faster gas exchange.
A thicker shell (0.5 mm here) increases the diffusion distance and slows diffusion.
The concentration gradient of oxygen (high in air, low in embryo) and of carbon dioxide (the reverse) drives diffusion; a steeper gradient speeds it up.
Higher temperature increases the kinetic energy of gas molecules, increasing the rate of diffusion.
Pore size and the moisture of the shell membrane also affect how easily gases pass through.

questions.question: The magnification of the membrane diagram is 1 x 10^7 and structure T is 2 units long on the diagram. Which unit is the actual length of T? Options: A cm, B mm, C m, D nm.
questions.answer: D (nm).
steps: Magnification = image size / actual size, so actual size = image size / magnification.
Taking the diagram unit as cm: 2 cm / 1 x 10^7 = 2 x 10^-7 cm.
Since 1 cm = 1 x 10^7 nm, the result 2 x 10^-7 cm equals 2 nm.
1 cm = 10^7 nm, so 2 x 10^-7 cm = 2 nm, a sensible size for a membrane component, so the unit is nm.

questions.question: Which structures in the membrane diagram contain a phosphate group? Options: A Q and R, B Q and T, C R and S, D S and T.
questions.answer: B: Q and T.
steps: Q is the head of a phospholipid, which contains the phosphate group.
T is a whole phospholipid molecule (head plus fatty acid tails), so it contains a phosphate group too.
R is a fatty acid tail and S is cholesterol, and neither contains phosphate, so options A, C and D are wrong.

questions.question: Which ratio of structures in the membrane diagram affects the fluidity of the membrane? Options: A Q:T, B R:Q, C R:T, D S:T.
questions.answer: D: S : T.
steps: S is cholesterol and T is a phospholipid.
The ratio of cholesterol to phospholipid sets how much cholesterol restricts the movement of the phospholipids, so it affects fluidity.

questions.question: Explain the role of the primary structure in determining the properties of the membrane protein labelled in the diagram.
questions.answer: The primary structure is the sequence of amino acids, which fixes the R groups; these determine bonding and folding, and so the protein's shape and whether it is hydrophobic or hydrophilic.
steps: The primary structure is the specific sequence of amino acids joined by peptide bonds.
The sequence determines the R groups, which can be hydrophobic or hydrophilic.
Hydrophobic R groups face the lipid core of the membrane, while hydrophilic ones face the water-based surface.
The sequence also determines the bonds that form the secondary and tertiary structure, so the protein's shape and function depend on it.

questions.question: Explain why each of the molecules in a table and diagram of molecules inside and outside a cell enters the cell by a different mechanism.
questions.answer: E (water) enters by osmosis, F (large polar) by facilitated diffusion, G (non-polar) by simple diffusion through the bilayer and H (small polar) by active transport.
steps: E is water: it is small and dipolar, and the numbers are similar inside and outside (about 5 each side), so it enters by osmosis through the bilayer or aquaporins, depending on water potential.

F is large and polar, so it cannot cross the hydrophobic core; there are more outside than inside (about 5 outside and 2 inside), so it enters by facilitated diffusion down its gradient through a channel or carrier protein, with no ATP.

G is non-polar, so it dissolves in the hydrophobic core of the phospholipid bilayer; it is more concentrated outside (about 4 against 1), so it enters by simple diffusion down its concentration gradient with no protein or ATP.

H is small and polar, so it cannot diffuse through the bilayer; it is more concentrated inside (about 12 inside against 3 outside), so it must enter against its concentration gradient by active transport using a carrier protein and ATP.

questions.question: Using the shapes showing the components of a phospholipid, draw a diagram to show its structure.
questions.answer: A phosphate circle joined by a bond (line) to a glycerol square, with two fatty acid rectangles each joined to the glycerol by a bond.
steps: Draw the circle (phosphate group) at the top and join it with a line (covalent bond) to the square (glycerol) below it.
Join two long rectangles (fatty acids) to the glycerol square, each with its own line, so that they hang parallel to each other away from the head.
The glycerol must have three attachments in total: one phosphate and two fatty acids (not three fatty acids).

questions.question: Which type of bond is found in a phospholipid molecule? Options: A ester, B glycosidic, C hydrogen, D peptide.
questions.answer: A (ester bond).
steps: Fatty acids are joined to the glycerol backbone of a phospholipid by ester bonds, formed in condensation reactions.
Glycosidic bonds join sugars, and peptide bonds join amino acids, so B and D are wrong.
Ester bonds link the fatty acids to the glycerol backbone of a phospholipid.
Hydrogen bonds are weak attractions, not covalent bonds that make up the molecule's structure.

questions.question: How does a non-polar molecule move through a cell membrane, down a concentration gradient, into a cell? Options: A active transport, B diffusion, C exocytosis, D osmosis.
questions.answer: B (diffusion).
steps: Non-polar molecules dissolve in the hydrophobic core of the phospholipid bilayer.
They move down their concentration gradient without energy, which is simple diffusion.
It then passes through the bilayer without carrier proteins.
Active transport needs ATP, exocytosis moves things out, and osmosis is only for water.

questions.question: How many of three statements about endocytosis are correct: (1) it transports substances out of the cell, (2) the cell membrane surrounds the substance, (3) it can only transport substances down a concentration gradient? Options: A none, B one, C two, D three.
questions.answer: B (one: only statement 2 is correct).
steps: Statement 1 describes exocytosis, which moves substances out, so it is wrong for endocytosis.
Statement 2 is correct: the cell surface membrane folds round the substance to form a vesicle.
Endocytosis forms a vesicle, which requires energy from ATP.
Statement 3 is wrong because endocytosis is an active process using ATP and can move substances against a gradient.

questions.question: Using the table showing one way the components of phospholipids can be drawn, draw a diagram of a phospholipid.
questions.answer: A glycerol bar with the phosphate circle joined to it by a bond on one side, and two fatty acid rectangles each joined to the glycerol by a bond on the other side.
steps: Draw the tall hatched rectangle (glycerol) in the centre.
Join the circle (phosphate group) to the glycerol with a short line (bond).
Join two of the long rectangles (fatty acids) to the glycerol, each with its own bond line, parallel to each other and pointing away from the phosphate.

questions.question: Which of the diagrams shows an ester bond, one of the bonds present in phospholipids?
steps: An ester bond is C-O-C with a C=O on the second carbon (the carbonyl), formed when a fatty acid joins to the glycerol hydroxyl group.
A and D contain nitrogen (peptide-type or N-O links), and B has no oxygen link between the carbons, so only C shows an ester bond.

questions.question: Explain why an increase in temperature increases the fluidity of the membrane.
questions.answer: Higher temperature gives phospholipids more kinetic energy, so they move more freely and the membrane becomes more fluid.
steps: Increasing temperature increases the kinetic energy of the phospholipid molecules.
The molecules vibrate and move more, so they slide past one another more easily.
The increased movement weakens the hydrophobic interactions between the fatty acid tails.
This makes the bilayer more fluid, with more movement of molecules and proteins within it.

questions.question: Which row of the table describes an unsaturated fatty acid compared with a saturated fatty acid with the same number of carbon atoms?
questions.answer: C: has double bonds between two carbons, with fewer hydrogens than the saturated fatty acid.
steps: An unsaturated fatty acid has at least one C=C double bond, so "yes" for double bonds.
Each double bond means two fewer hydrogen atoms for the same number of carbons, so it has fewer hydrogens than the saturated one.

questions.question: Explain why a decrease in cholesterol increases the fluidity of the membrane.
questions.answer: Cholesterol packs between the phospholipid fatty acid tails and restricts their movement, so less cholesterol means the phospholipids can move more freely.
steps: Cholesterol sits between the phospholipid tails in the bilayer.
Its rigid steroid rings restrict the movement of the fatty acid chains.
Cholesterol is a rigid molecule that restricts the movement of the fatty acid tails.
When cholesterol decreases, there is less restriction, so the phospholipids move more and the membrane is more fluid.

questions.question: Suggest why a fatty acid with a shorter side chain increases the fluidity of a membrane.
questions.answer: Shorter chains have fewer carbon atoms, so fewer van der Waals forces hold neighbouring tails together, and they pack less tightly, so the membrane is more fluid.
steps: Each carbon-carbon chain contributes intermolecular (van der Waals) attractions with its neighbours.
A shorter chain has fewer such attractions, so the tails are held together less strongly.
Shorter tails therefore pack less tightly, so the bilayer is more fluid.
The tails therefore pack less tightly and move more easily, increasing fluidity.

questions.question: Suggest how the content of fatty acids in the fish membranes may have changed after the fish were moved into water at a lower temperature.
questions.answer: The membranes would contain more unsaturated fatty acids (and shorter chains), which keep the membrane fluid at lower temperature.
steps: At lower temperature the membrane would become less fluid and more rigid, because molecules have less kinetic energy.
Unsaturated fatty acids have kinks at their double bonds, which prevent tight packing.
Unsaturated fatty acids have double bonds that put kinks in the chains, preventing tight packing.
So the fish increase the proportion of unsaturated (and shorter) fatty acids in their membranes.

questions.question: Suggest why these changes in fatty acid content are necessary for the survival of the fish.
questions.answer: A fluid membrane keeps membrane proteins such as enzymes and transporters working at low temperature, so the cells can still function.
steps: Membrane proteins, including enzymes and carrier proteins, need a fluid membrane to change shape and work.
If the membrane became too rigid, transport and metabolic reactions would slow down.
Without this adjustment the membrane would become rigid at low temperature.
Keeping the membrane fluid at low temperature maintains these processes and so keeps the fish alive.

questions.question: Describe the evidence for and against a relationship between blood cholesterol levels and heart disease, from the graph of a 10-year study.
questions.answer: For: the group that developed heart disease has its peak at a higher cholesterol level, and more of them have high levels. Against: the two distributions overlap greatly, so many people with high cholesterol did not develop heart disease and many with low cholesterol did.
steps: Evidence for: the peak of the dashed line (developed heart disease) is at a higher blood cholesterol level than the peak of the solid line, and at the highest levels the dashed line is above the solid line.
Evidence for: at low cholesterol levels the solid line (did not develop disease) is higher than the dashed line.
Evidence against: the two curves overlap over almost the whole range and have similar shapes and heights, so many people in both groups had the same cholesterol level.
Evidence against: the difference between the two peaks is small, and there is no cholesterol level that separates the groups, so cholesterol is not the only factor.

questions.question: Describe the evidence in the graph of HDL and LDL levels and CVD incidence that supports three given conclusions.
questions.answer: Incidence of CVD rises with LDL level, falls with HDL level, and is highest when HDL is low and LDL is high.
steps: LDL: for every HDL group the bars get taller as the LDL level goes from <100 to >=160 mg dm-3, for example at HDL <40 from about 2 a.u. to the tallest bar (about 7 a.u.).
HDL: for every LDL group the bars get shorter as the HDL level goes from <40 to >=60 mg dm-3.

Ratio: the tallest bars (above about 6 a.u.) are at low HDL and high LDL, the lowest ratio of HDL to LDL, whereas the shortest bars (below about 1 a.u.) are at HDL >=60 and LDL <100, the highest ratio.

questions.question: Explain how the LDL receptor (LDL-R), a surface protein on liver cells, is involved in endocytosis of LDLs.
questions.answer: LDL-R binds LDL on the outer surface, the complex is taken into the cell in a coated vesicle by endocytosis, delivering LDL and cholesterol into the cell.
steps: The LDL-R on the cell surface membrane has a binding site that is complementary to the LDL particle.
LDL binds to the receptor, and the receptors cluster in a coated pit on the membrane.
The membrane folds in around the complex, forming an endocytotic vesicle that enters the cell.
Inside the cell the LDL is released and the cholesterol is used by the cell.

questions.topic: pH Separation of LDL and Receptor
questions.question: Suggest how a lower pH inside the cell could cause the LDL to separate from its receptor.
questions.answer: A lower pH changes the ionisation of amino acid R groups at the binding site, altering the protein's tertiary structure and breaking the bonds that hold LDL to the receptor.
steps: The binding between LDL and the receptor depends on ionic and hydrogen bonds between R groups.
Lower pH changes the charge (ionisation) of these R groups.
A lower pH means more H+ ions, which change the charge of acidic and basic R groups.
This changes the tertiary structure of the receptor's binding site, so the bonds with LDL break and the LDL is released.

questions.question: Explain why mutations in the gene coding for the LDL-R can increase the risk of cardiovascular disease.
questions.answer: A mutated receptor may not bind LDL or be endocytosed, so LDL stays in the blood, raising blood cholesterol and promoting atherosclerosis.
steps: A mutation in the LDL-R gene can change the receptor's amino acid sequence and shape.
The faulty receptor may not bind LDL properly, or may fail to be taken into the cell by endocytosis.
LDL then stays in the blood, so blood cholesterol levels rise.
The LDL can deposit cholesterol in artery walls, forming plaques that lead to atherosclerosis and CVD.

questions.question: In a Venn diagram comparing diffusion, facilitated diffusion and active transport, which part would contain the statement 'uses proteins'? Options: A II, B III, C IV, D VII.
questions.answer: D: Part VII.
steps: Simple diffusion does not use proteins, but facilitated diffusion (channel and carrier proteins) and active transport (carrier pumps) do.
The part shared by active transport and facilitated diffusion only (outside the diffusion circle) is Part VII.

questions.question: In the Venn diagram, which part would contain the statement 'needs energy in the form of ATP'? Options: A II, B V, C VI, D VII.
questions.answer: B: Part V.
steps: Only active transport needs ATP; diffusion and facilitated diffusion are passive.
The part that belongs to the active transport circle only is Part V.

questions.question: In the Venn diagram, which part would contain the statement 'solutes can only move down a concentration gradient'? Options: A II, B III, C V, D VII.
questions.answer: B: Part III.
steps: Solutes move only down a concentration gradient in diffusion and in facilitated diffusion, but active transport can move them against it.
The part shared by diffusion and facilitated diffusion only (not active transport) is Part III.

questions.question: Explain the definition of osmosis: the movement of free water molecules through a partially permeable membrane, down a water potential gradient.
questions.answer: Osmosis is the net movement of free water molecules from a region of higher water potential to lower water potential across a partially permeable membrane, which lets water but not large solutes pass.
steps: Free water molecules are those not bound to solutes, and they move randomly in both directions.
A partially permeable membrane lets water through but not dissolved solutes.
Water potential is higher in dilute solutions and lower in concentrated solutions, so water moves from high to low water potential.
Movement is down the water potential gradient, so there is a net movement of water until equilibrium is reached.

questions.topic: Crab Muscle Water and Amino Acid Changes
questions.question: Explain the changes in water content and amino acid content in the muscle cells of mitten crabs moved from fresh water into sea water, using the graph.
questions.answer: Sea water has a lower water potential than the crab cells, so water leaves the muscle cells by osmosis and the water content falls; the cells then raise their amino acid content, lowering their own water potential, so water re-enters and the water content recovers.
steps: Water content falls quickly from about 76% to about 74% in the first day, reaching a minimum of about 73.8% at about 4.5 days, because the sea water has a higher salt concentration (lower water potential) than the muscle cells, so water leaves them by osmosis.

Amino acid content rises from about 228 a.u. to about 335 a.u. over the 15 days, steeply at first then more slowly, so the crab increases the solute concentration inside its cells (amino acids are made or released by protein breakdown).
More solutes lower the water potential of the cell contents, reducing the water potential gradient between the cell and the sea water.
This lets water move back into the cells by osmosis, so water content slowly rises again to about 75% by 15 days.
The crab is osmoregulating (becoming an osmoconformer), so the cell solute concentration approaches that of the sea water and the rate of change slows as equilibrium is approached.

questions.question: A hydra has a body length of 1.8 mm and diameter of 1 mm. Which is the magnification of the drawing? Options: A 3.75 x 10^-2, B 3.75 x 10^-1, C 2.67 x 10^0, D 2.67 x 10^1.
questions.answer: D: 2.67 x 10^1 (about 27 times).
steps: Measure the length of the body on the drawing: it is about 5 cm (50 mm) from the bracket.
Magnification = drawing length / actual length = 50 mm / 1.8 mm = about 28, which matches 2.67 x 10^1 (that is, 48 mm / 1.8 mm).
The other options are far too small: for example 2.67 would make the 1.8 mm body only about 5 mm long on the drawing, and 0.0375 and 0.375 would make the drawing smaller than the animal.

questions.question: Using surface area = 2 pi r l, which is the surface area in mm2 of a hydra with body length 1.8 mm and diameter 1 mm? Options: A 0.9 pi, B 1.8 pi, C 3.6 pi, D 5.4 pi.
questions.answer: B (1.8 pi mm2).
steps: The radius is half the diameter: r = 1 / 2 = 0.5 mm.
Length l = 1.8 mm.
The formula gives the curved surface area of a cylinder, which models the hydra body.
Surface area = 2 x pi x 0.5 x 1.8 = 1.8 pi mm2, which is option B.

questions.topic: Surface Area to Volume Ratio of Hydra
questions.question: Another hydra has a surface area of 2.3 pi mm2, a body length of 1.8 mm and a diameter of 1.2 mm. Calculate its surface area to volume ratio, using volume = pi r^2 l.
steps: Radius = 1.2 / 2 = 0.6 mm.
Volume = pi x 0.6^2 x 1.8 = 0.648 pi mm3.
Ratio = surface area / volume = 2.3 pi / 0.648 pi = 3.55, which is 3.5 mm-1 to two significant figures.
Using the given surface area is required here, although 2 pi r l with these dimensions gives 2.16 pi.

questions.question: Explain how a hydra, with a hollow body made of two layers of cells, is adapted for gas exchange.
questions.answer: The body wall is only two cells thick and every cell is close to the water, so oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse across a short distance with no need for a transport system.
steps: The hydra body wall is only two cells thick, so the diffusion distance is very short.
Each cell is in direct contact with the surrounding water or the hollow body cavity, so every cell can exchange gases.
Its cylindrical body gives a relatively large surface area to volume ratio for diffusion.
Oxygen diffuses in and carbon dioxide diffuses out down concentration gradients, so no specialised gas exchange organ is needed.

questions.question: Name the law on which the formula for the rate of diffusion (depending on surface area, diffusion distance and concentration gradient) is based.
questions.answer: Fick's law.
steps: Rate of diffusion = surface area x concentration gradient / diffusion distance.
This relationship is Fick's law.
It states that rate is proportional to surface area and concentration gradient, and inversely proportional to distance.
It explains why gas exchange surfaces are thin and large.

questions.question: What happens to the rate of diffusion if the surface area is halved, the concentration gradient is halved and the diffusion distance is halved at the same time? Options: A stays the same, B a quarter of its value, C halves, D doubles.
questions.answer: C (it halves).
steps: Rate is proportional to surface area x concentration gradient / diffusion distance.
Halving surface area multiplies the rate by 0.5, and halving the gradient multiplies it by 0.5.
Each change multiplies the rate separately, so the effects combine multiplicatively.
Halving the diffusion distance doubles the rate (multiplies by 2): 0.5 x 0.5 x 2 = 0.5, so the rate halves.

questions.question: Describe how mammalian lungs are adapted to have a large surface area, a short diffusion distance and a high concentration gradient.
questions.answer: Many alveoli give a large surface area; alveolar and capillary walls are one cell thick for a short diffusion distance; ventilation and blood flow maintain a high concentration gradient.
steps: Large surface area: millions of alveoli provide a huge total surface area for exchange.
Short diffusion distance: alveolar walls and capillary walls are each only one cell thick.
High concentration gradient: ventilation keeps alveolar oxygen high and carbon dioxide low.
The blood flow through the capillaries removes oxygen and supplies carbon dioxide, keeping the gradient steep.

questions.question: Discuss how the structure and behaviour of the hellbender salamander are adapted for gas exchange, using the graph of body rocking frequency, blood pO2 and percentage saturation of the water.
questions.answer: The hellbender has skin folds and thin skin that give a large surface area for gas exchange, and it rocks its body to bring fresh oxygenated water over the skin, rocking most when the water has only 25% oxygen saturation.
steps: Structure: the skin folds greatly increase the surface area, and a thin skin with many capillaries gives a short diffusion distance; it also has lungs, so it uses two gas exchange surfaces.
Behaviour: body rocking and swaying moves water over the skin, replacing the water next to the skin that has lost its oxygen and so keeping the oxygen concentration gradient steep for diffusion.
Data: blood pO2 rises sharply from about 0.8 kPa at 0% water saturation to about 3.5 kPa at 25%, then increases only slightly to about 3.9 kPa at 100%.

Rocking frequency rises from about 5 per minute at 0% to a maximum of about 8.5 per minute at 25% saturation, then falls to about 4 per minute at 75 to 100% saturation, because when the water holds plenty of oxygen less rocking is needed.
At 0% saturation rocking is lower than at 25%, since there is little oxygen to obtain; the hellbender also lives in shallow, fast-flowing, well-oxygenated streams, which helps its skin gas exchange.

questions.question: From the graph of solute concentration of cells of marine animals P, Q and R, which row of the table identifies them?
questions.answer: B: P partial osmoconformer, Q strict osmoconformer, R osmoregulator.
steps: R is a flat line: the cell solute concentration stays constant whatever the sea water concentration, so it is an osmoregulator.
Q is a steep straight line rising with sea water concentration, so the cell solute concentration matches that of the sea water: a strict osmoconformer.
P rises only slightly at first and then follows the sea water at higher concentrations, so its cell concentration varies with the sea water only partly: a partial osmoconformer.

questions.question: Explain the advantages for osmoconformers of having cells with solute concentrations similar to that of the sea water they live in.
questions.answer: Cell and sea water concentrations match, so there is no net water movement by osmosis and no energy is needed to regulate water or ion balance.
steps: If cell and sea water solute concentrations are equal, there is no water potential gradient, so no net osmosis occurs.
The animal does not gain or lose water, so it avoids the risk of swelling or dehydration.
Osmoconformers therefore keep a stable cell volume without active regulation.
Because it does not need to pump ions or water to maintain balance, it saves energy that can be used for growth and activity.

questions.question: Estimate the chloride ion concentration of the cells of a jellyfish from the table of ion concentrations in sea water and in osmoconformers.
questions.answer: About 557 a.u. (accept about 550 to 558 a.u.).
steps: The jellyfish is an osmoconformer, so its ion concentrations are close to those in the sea water (chloride 558).
Its other ions are about the same as the sea water and the sea urchin (chloride 557), so chloride should be about 557 a.u.

questions.question: Calculate the percentage difference in the concentration of magnesium ions in the lobster compared with the sea urchin, to two decimal places.
steps: Magnesium: lobster = 9 a.u. and sea urchin = 54 a.u.
Difference = 9 - 54 = -45 a.u.
Percentage difference compared with the sea urchin = -45 / 54 x 100 = -83.33%, that is 83.33% lower in the lobster.

questions.question: Explain why these three animals are osmoconformers even though they have different concentrations of each ion in their cells.
questions.answer: The total solute concentration (water potential) of their cells matches the sea water, so there is no net water movement, even though the individual ions differ.
steps: An osmoconformer is defined by its total cell solute concentration matching sea water.
Different ions can be balanced by other solutes, such as amino acids and organic molecules, so the total is the same as the sea water.
Total solute concentration is the property that controls osmosis, not each ion separately.
With equal total solute concentrations there is no water potential gradient, so no net water movement.

questions.question: Suggest why osmoconformers do not have the same concentration of each ion in their cells.
questions.answer: Only the total solute concentration needs to match the sea water; the balance of individual ions can be different, with other solutes such as amino acids making up the difference.
steps: Osmoconformers only need to match total solute concentration to avoid water movement.
Individual ions can vary because other solutes, such as amino acids, can replace them to balance the total.
Ions and amino acids differ in permeability and function, so their levels vary.
Each ion's permeability and function may also differ, so each is kept at a different level.

questions.question: Energy is needed to maintain the concentration of ions inside the osmoconformers. Explain what this energy is used for.
questions.answer: The energy (ATP from respiration) is used for active transport, pumping ions across the cell membrane against their concentration gradients.
steps: Ions are moved across membranes against their concentration gradients.
This requires energy from ATP, which is produced by respiration.
Maintaining these gradients is active, because it stops ions leaking down their concentration gradients.
Carrier proteins, such as the sodium-potassium pump, use the energy to move the ions and keep the concentrations different from the sea water.

questions.question: Which option describes a phospholipid? Options: A hydrophilic fatty acid head and hydrophobic phosphate tails, B hydrophilic phosphate head and hydrophobic fatty acid tails, C hydrophobic fatty acid head and hydrophilic phosphate tails, D hydrophobic phosphate head and hydrophilic fatty acid tails.
questions.answer: B.
steps: A phospholipid has a phosphate-containing head that is hydrophilic (attracted to water).
It has two fatty acid tails that are hydrophobic (repel water).
The hydrophilic heads face the water on both sides of the bilayer.
So option B is the correct description.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the structure of the Davson-Danielli model with the fluid mosaic model of membrane structure.
questions.answer: Both have a phospholipid bilayer with proteins; Davson-Danielli has proteins as layers coating the surfaces and a rigid structure, while fluid mosaic has proteins embedded and scattered in a fluid bilayer.
steps: Similarity: both models describe a phospholipid bilayer with proteins associated with it.
Davson-Danielli: the proteins form continuous layers on the outer and inner surfaces of the bilayer, sandwiching it.
Fluid mosaic: the proteins are embedded in the bilayer and scattered in a mosaic, some spanning the whole membrane.
Fluid mosaic: the phospholipids can move laterally, so the membrane is fluid and dynamic, whereas Davson-Danielli describes a rigid, static structure.

questions.question: Suggest how damage to the cell membrane could result in cell death.
questions.answer: Damage lets substances leak in and out uncontrolled, so concentration gradients and ion balance are lost, and the cell may swell, burst or stop functioning.
steps: The membrane controls which substances enter and leave; damage removes this control.
Ions and molecules leak across, destroying concentration gradients needed for cell processes.
Water may enter by osmosis, causing swelling and lysis, or enzymes and organelles may be lost.
Loss of these functions stops the cell from carrying out its processes, causing death.

questions.question: Explain why parts of the membrane around the edge of damage are able to fuse together to repair the damage.
questions.answer: Phospholipids are free to move, so the edges can rearrange and the hydrophobic tails and hydrophilic heads align to rejoin into a continuous bilayer.
steps: The phospholipid bilayer is fluid, so phospholipids at the edges can move.
The hydrophilic heads face water on both sides, and the hydrophobic tails face each other.
The membrane must be fluid so that the edges can move together.
When the edges are brought together, these interactions allow the bilayer to reform and fuse into a continuous membrane.

questions.question: Once the membrane has fused, suggest what else the cell needs to do to complete the repair of the membrane.
questions.answer: The cell must replace the lost membrane proteins and glycoproteins, which are made on ribosomes and delivered by vesicles from the Golgi, and restore the membrane's composition.
steps: Membrane proteins and glycoproteins may have been lost or damaged in the injury.
Ribosomes on the rough ER make the replacement proteins, which are modified in the Golgi.
Vesicles fuse with the membrane to deliver the lipids and proteins needed to complete the repair.
Golgi vesicles carry the new proteins and lipids to the damaged area and insert them into the membrane.

questions.question: Why do phospholipids form a bilayer? Options: A hydrophobic heads dissolve in water, B hydrophobic heads move away from water, C hydrophobic tails dissolve in water, D hydrophobic tails move away from water.
questions.answer: D (the hydrophobic tails move away from the aqueous environment).
steps: Phospholipid tails are hydrophobic and cannot dissolve in water.
In water the tails are shielded by arranging into a bilayer, with the hydrophilic heads facing water.
Forming a bilayer minimises contact between the tails and water, which is energetically favourable.
Options A, B and C are wrong because the heads are hydrophilic and the tails are hydrophobic.

questions.question: From the diagram of part of a cell membrane, which letter (P, Q, R or S) represents a membrane glycoprotein?
questions.answer: B: Q.
steps: A glycoprotein is a protein with a carbohydrate chain attached.
Q is the large protein with a branched carbohydrate chain attached, while P has the carbohydrate chain attached to a phospholipid head, so P is a glycolipid.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term osmosis.
questions.answer: The net movement of water molecules from a region of higher water potential to a region of lower water potential across a partially permeable membrane.
steps: Osmosis is the net movement (diffusion) of water molecules only.
It takes place across a partially permeable membrane, which lets water through but not larger solute molecules.
Water moves from a region of higher water potential (more dilute solution) to a region of lower water potential (more concentrated solution).
It is a passive process: it is down the water potential gradient and needs no energy from ATP.

questions.question: Compare and contrast exocytosis and endocytosis.
questions.answer: Both are active processes using vesicles and ATP; endocytosis brings substances into the cell, while exocytosis moves them out.
steps: Similarity: both involve vesicles that fuse with or form from the cell surface membrane and both need ATP.
Difference: endocytosis takes substances into the cell by the membrane folding round them to form a vesicle.
Endocytosis and exocytosis are both forms of bulk transport using vesicles.
Difference: exocytosis releases substances out of the cell when a vesicle fuses with the cell surface membrane.

questions.question: Explain why oxygen molecules can pass directly through the cell membrane.
questions.answer: Oxygen is small and non-polar, so it dissolves in the hydrophobic core of the bilayer and diffuses straight through down its concentration gradient without energy.
steps: Oxygen is a small, non-polar molecule.
It can dissolve in the hydrophobic core of the phospholipid bilayer.
Because it needs no ATP or carrier, it is not active transport.
It diffuses across the membrane down its concentration gradient, so no carrier protein or energy is needed.

questions.topic: Human Lung Adaptations for Rapid Gas Exchange
questions.question: Explain how human lungs are adapted for rapid gas exchange.
questions.answer: Millions of alveoli give a large surface area, thin one-cell walls and a dense capillary network give short diffusion distances, and ventilation keeps a steep concentration gradient.
steps: The many alveoli give a very large surface area for gas exchange.
The alveolar and capillary walls are one cell thick, giving a short diffusion distance.
A dense capillary network around each alveolus keeps the blood moving and maintains a steep concentration gradient.
Ventilation continually replaces alveolar air, keeping oxygen high and carbon dioxide low.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term allele.
questions.answer: An alternative form of a gene, found at the same locus on a chromosome.
steps: A gene is a section of DNA that codes for a polypeptide.
An allele is one of the different versions of that gene.
Different alleles of a gene can produce different versions of the same protein.
Alleles occupy the same position (locus) on homologous chromosomes.

questions.question: The CFTR protein coded for by the F508 mutation has one missing amino acid. Explain how this mutation results in a non-functioning CFTR protein.
questions.answer: Deleting three bases removes one amino acid, which changes the primary structure; the protein then misfolds, so its tertiary shape and channel are lost and it does not function.
steps: The F508 mutation deletes three bases in the DNA, so one codon is lost.
This means one amino acid is missing from the polypeptide, changing the primary structure.
The change in primary structure alters the bonds that determine folding, so the CFTR protein misfolds.
The misfolded protein cannot function as a chloride channel and is often destroyed, so it does not reach the cell surface membrane.

questions.question: Explain why people with cystic fibrosis may develop lung infections.
questions.answer: Without functional CFTR, chloride is not secreted and water does not follow, so the mucus becomes thick and sticky; cilia cannot clear it, so bacteria accumulate and cause infection.
steps: The CFTR channel normally transports chloride ions out of cells into the airway surface.
Water follows by osmosis, keeping the mucus thin and watery.
With non-functioning CFTR, less water enters the mucus, so it becomes thick and sticky.
Thick mucus traps bacteria and cannot be cleared by cilia, so bacteria multiply and cause lung infections.

questions.question: State the property of the cell membrane that enables an amoeba to change shape by pushing cytoplasm against it to form long thin projections.
questions.answer: Fluidity (the membrane is flexible because phospholipids can move past each other).
steps: The cell surface membrane is a fluid phospholipid bilayer rather than a rigid structure.
Phospholipids and proteins can move, so the membrane stretches and deforms.
Fluidity is what allows the amoeba to form pseudopodia.
This flexibility allows the amoeba to form pseudopodia.

questions.question: The amoeba in Shape 1 is roughly spherical. Using surface area of a sphere = 4 pi r^2, which is its surface area? Options: A 90 000 m2, B 90 000 m3, C 360 000 m2, D 360 000 m3.
steps: The diameter of Shape 1 is 300 um, so r = 150 um.
Surface area = 4 x pi x 150^2 = 4 x pi x 22 500 = 90 000 pi um^2.
An area is in um^2, so B and D (um^3) are wrong, and C (360 000 pi) comes from using the diameter instead of the radius.

questions.topic: Surface Area and Volume Change to Shape 2
questions.question: The mass of the amoeba stays the same when it changes from Shape 1 to Shape 2. Which row of the table shows what happens to its surface area and volume?
questions.answer: C: surface area increases, volume stays the same.
steps: The mass of the amoeba is unchanged, so its volume stays the same.
Shape 2 has long thin projections, so its surface area is larger than that of a sphere of the same volume.

questions.question: Explain why an amoeba can rely on diffusion to supply the oxygen it needs.
questions.answer: The amoeba is small with a large surface area to volume ratio, so the diffusion distance to every part of the cell is short and diffusion is fast enough.
steps: The amoeba is a single small cell, so the distance from membrane to the centre is short.
Its surface area to volume ratio is large, so there is enough membrane for the oxygen it needs.
Its membrane area is large relative to its volume.
Diffusion over this short distance is fast enough to supply oxygen and remove carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Which pair of membrane transport mechanisms only involves a solute moving down a concentration gradient? Options: A active transport and diffusion, B active transport and osmosis, C diffusion and facilitated diffusion, D facilitated diffusion and osmosis.
questions.answer: C (diffusion and facilitated diffusion).
steps: Diffusion and facilitated diffusion both move solutes passively down a concentration gradient.
Active transport moves solutes against the gradient, so A and B are wrong.
Facilitated diffusion also moves solutes down a gradient, using channel or carrier proteins without ATP.
Osmosis moves water, not a solute, so D is wrong.

questions.question: Which transport mechanisms involve carrier proteins in the membrane, among active transport, diffusion and exocytosis? Options: A active transport only, B active transport and exocytosis, C diffusion only, D diffusion and exocytosis.
questions.answer: A (active transport only).
steps: Active transport uses carrier proteins that bind a solute and change shape to move it against its gradient.
Simple diffusion does not involve any membrane protein, and exocytosis uses vesicles, not carriers.
Diffusion through the bilayer requires no protein at all.
So only active transport involves carrier proteins.

questions.question: Which cell transport mechanism is used to take large particles or bacteria into a cell? Options: A active transport, B endocytosis, C exocytosis, D facilitated diffusion.
questions.answer: B (endocytosis).
steps: Endocytosis engulfs material by folding the cell surface membrane round it to form a vesicle.
This allows large particles and bacteria to enter the cell.
Phagocytosis is a form of endocytosis for solid particles.
Exocytosis moves material out, and the other options use carriers or pumps for small molecules.

questions.question: Which cell transport mechanism moves small lipid-soluble molecules through the membrane? Options: A active transport, B diffusion, C facilitated diffusion, D osmosis.
questions.answer: B (diffusion).
steps: Small lipid-soluble molecules dissolve in the phospholipid bilayer.
They pass straight through by simple diffusion, without carrier proteins.
The hydrophobic core of the bilayer lets these molecules pass without help.
Facilitated diffusion is for polar or charged molecules, and osmosis is only for water.

questions.topic: Charge on Channel Protein R Groups
questions.question: Which row of the table describes the charge on the R groups on the amino acids of a channel protein used in facilitated diffusion?
questions.answer: B: polar R groups face inside the channel and non-polar R groups face the rest of the membrane.
steps: The channel contains water and ions, so the R groups lining it are polar (hydrophilic) and attract them.
The rest of the protein is in contact with the hydrophobic fatty acid tails, so those R groups are non-polar (hydrophobic).

questions.question: Explain the results of an investigation in which pieces of sweet potato were placed in four coloured dye solutions and their mass change was measured.
questions.answer: The sweet potato lost mass in purple and orange, gained mass in red and did not change in blue, because of the water potential of each solution compared with the sweet potato cells.
steps: Orange: mass falls from about 1.12 g to about 0.50 g (about 55% loss): the solution has the lowest water potential, so water leaves the cells by osmosis from a large gradient.
Purple: mass falls from 1.00 g to about 0.87 g (about 13% loss): the solution has a lower water potential than the cells, but the gradient is smaller, so less water leaves by osmosis.
Red: mass rises from 1.00 g to about 1.39 g (about 39% gain): the solution has a higher water potential than the cell contents, so water enters by osmosis.
Blue: mass stays at 1.00 g: the water potential of the solution equals that of the cells, so there is no net movement of water.

questions.question: From the diagram of a human heart with vessels labelled P, Q, R and S, which pair transports blood to and from the lungs? Options: A P and Q, B Q and S, C R and P, D S and R.
questions.answer: B: Q and S.
steps: Q is the pulmonary artery, taking deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs.
S is the pulmonary vein, bringing oxygenated blood from the lungs back to the heart.
P is the vena cava and R is the aorta, so they do not go to the lungs.

questions.question: From the labelled heart diagram (P, Q, R, S), which pair of vessels is chosen from options A P, B P and R, C Q, D Q and R?
questions.answer: A: P.
steps: Veins have valves along their length to stop the backflow of blood, and P is the vena cava, a vein.
Q (pulmonary artery) and R (aorta) have valves only at their origin at the heart, not along their length.

questions.question: From the labelled heart diagram (options AP, BQ, CR, DS), which blood vessel does the coronary artery branch from?
questions.answer: C: R.
steps: The coronary arteries supply the heart muscle and branch from the aorta just above the aortic valve.
The aorta is vessel R.

questions.question: Name two other factors, besides diffusion distance, that affect the rate of diffusion between blood and cells.
questions.answer: Surface area and concentration gradient (temperature is also acceptable).
steps: Rate of diffusion increases with a larger surface area for exchange.
It increases with a steeper concentration gradient between the blood and the cells.
Both factors increase the rate of diffusion, while diffusion distance is the third factor.
Temperature also affects the rate, as higher temperature increases molecular kinetic energy.

questions.question: Name the law of diffusion that can be used to calculate the rate of diffusion.
questions.answer: Fick's law.
steps: Fick's law relates the rate of diffusion to surface area, concentration gradient and diffusion distance.
Fick's law is used to calculate rates, so it is the law the question asks for.
Rate = surface area x concentration gradient / diffusion distance (with a constant).
It applies to the diffusion of gases and solutes across membranes.

questions.question: Complete the table showing the time taken for a molecule to diffuse over different diffusion distances.
questions.answer: 100 um row: 5000 ms; 1 mm row: 1000 um and 498 000 ms (about 5 x 10^5 ms).
steps: 100 um takes 5.0 seconds, which is 5.0 x 1000 = 5000 milliseconds.
8.3 minutes = 8.3 x 60 = 498 seconds = 498 000 milliseconds (about 5 x 10^5 ms).

questions.question: Explain why it is important for body cells to be close to capillaries to meet the demands of respiration, using the information in the question and the table.
questions.answer: A short diffusion distance means oxygen reaches respiring cells quickly and carbon dioxide is removed quickly, since diffusion time increases with distance.
steps: Respiring cells need a continuous supply of oxygen for aerobic respiration to make ATP.
Oxygen must diffuse from the capillary blood into the cells across the tissue fluid.
The table shows that diffusion time increases as the diffusion distance increases, so a short distance gives a fast supply.
Being close to capillaries also keeps a steep concentration gradient, so oxygen supply meets the cells' demand.

questions.question: Explain the difference between the two types of solute suggested by Overton, and why only one type can cross the lipid membrane.
questions.answer: Lipid-soluble (non-polar) solutes dissolve in the hydrophobic core of the membrane and cross it, whereas polar or charged solutes cannot cross the hydrophobic core.
steps: Lipid-soluble solutes are non-polar, so they dissolve in the lipid-based core of the membrane.
Polar and charged solutes are not soluble in the hydrophobic core and cannot pass through it.
Overton explains why lipid-soluble substances enter cells more readily.
So only the lipid-soluble solutes can cross the lipid membrane.

questions.question: Explain why the phospholipids in a cell membrane cannot be arranged in a single layer, as Langmuir proposed.
questions.answer: The cell is surrounded by water on both sides, so a single layer would expose hydrophobic tails to water; a bilayer hides the tails and exposes the hydrophilic heads to water on both sides.
steps: The cell has water both inside and outside, so the membrane has aqueous environments on both faces.
In a single layer, the hydrophobic tails would be exposed to water on one side.
A bilayer keeps the hydrophobic tails away from water on both sides.
A bilayer with heads facing outwards and tails inwards hides the tails from water on both sides.

questions.question: Give two ways in which phospholipids can be different from each other, even though they are all arranged in a bilayer.
questions.answer: They can have different fatty acid tails (different chain lengths or saturation), and different head groups attached to the phosphate.
steps: Phospholipids can contain fatty acids of different chain lengths.
They can also have different degrees of saturation, with saturated or unsaturated fatty acid tails.
Changes in these fatty acids alter the fluidity of the membrane.
The polar head group attached to the phosphate can also vary between phospholipids.

questions.question: Explain why some membrane proteins would not be able to carry out their transport functions if they were located only on the surface of the phospholipid bilayer.
questions.answer: Transport proteins must span the bilayer to form a channel or carrier linking the inside and outside, which proteins on the surface cannot do.
steps: Transport proteins move solutes from one side of the membrane to the other.
They must therefore span the bilayer, forming a channel or binding site accessible from both sides.
A protein on one surface can only reach one side of the bilayer.
Proteins only on the surface cannot reach across the hydrophobic core, so they could not move solutes through the membrane.

questions.question: The thickness of the cell membranes between X and Y in the photograph is 22.8 nm. Calculate the magnification of the photograph, to two significant figures.
