questions.answer: About 2.6 x 10^5 (about 260 000 times).
steps: Measure the length of the line between X and Y on the photograph: about 6 mm.
Convert to nm: 6 mm = 6 x 10^6 nm.
Magnification = image size / actual size = 6 x 10^6 / 22.8 = 2.6 x 10^5 (2 s.f.).
The result depends on the measured length: 5.5 to 6.5 mm gives 2.4 x 10^5 to 2.9 x 10^5.

questions.question: Explain why the Singer and Nicolson model is called the fluid mosaic model.
questions.answer: It is fluid because phospholipids and proteins can move sideways within the bilayer, and a mosaic because proteins are scattered through it like tiles in a pattern.
steps: The phospholipid bilayer is fluid because the molecules can move laterally within each layer.
Proteins embedded in the bilayer can also move, so the membrane is dynamic.
The name describes both the fluid and the mosaic components of the membrane.
The proteins are scattered in a random pattern, like the pieces of a mosaic.

questions.topic: Changing Gas Exchange in Frog Development
questions.question: The contributions of lungs, gills and skin to gas exchange change as a tadpole develops into an adult frog. Explain the importance of these changes.
questions.answer: Gills are replaced by lungs as the frog grows and moves onto land, because lungs supply enough oxygen for a larger, more active adult, while skin still helps when moist.
steps: Tadpoles live in water and rely on gills, which are efficient in water.
As the frog develops and moves onto land, it needs lungs to take oxygen from air.
Lungs provide a large surface area that meets the greater oxygen demand of the larger, more active adult.
The skin remains a supplementary gas exchange surface, especially when the frog is moist or submerged.

questions.question: Give one similarity and one difference between the structure of a frog heart and a mammalian heart.
questions.answer: Similarity: both have two atria and a ventricle with valves. Difference: the frog has a single ventricle, whereas the mammal has two separate ventricles.
steps: Both hearts have atria that receive blood and ventricles that pump it out.
Both have valves that keep blood flowing in one direction.
A frog heart has one ventricle, so oxygenated and deoxygenated blood partly mix.
A mammalian heart has two separate ventricles, keeping the two circuits completely separate.

questions.question: Explain how the circulatory system and the gas exchange surfaces of an adult frog meet the oxygen needs of its cells, using the percentage blood flow diagram.
questions.answer: The adult frog meets its oxygen needs by passing blood through two gas exchange surfaces (lungs and skin) and returning it to the heart, where it is pumped on at higher pressure, with little mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood in the single ventricle.
steps: Gas exchange surfaces: 39% of the blood goes to the lungs and 17% to the skin, so 56% of the output passes through gas exchange surfaces; the lungs have a large surface area, and the thin moist skin has a short diffusion distance, so oxygen is taken up by two surfaces.

Double circulation: blood goes back to the heart after the lungs (39%) and the skin (61% returns in total), so it is pumped again at higher pressure to the tissues, giving faster flow to the cells than it would after passing through the capillaries only once.

Separation of the blood: of the 44% going to the cells, 35 parts come from the oxygenated blood returning from the lungs and only 9 from the right atrium; of the 56% going to the lungs and skin, 52 parts come from the right atrium and only 4 from the lung blood.

So the ventricle gives mostly oxygenated blood to the cells (about 80% of that blood comes from the lungs) and mostly deoxygenated blood to the lungs and skin, so the blood supply to the cells is rich in oxygen.
The skin also gives extra oxygen while the frog is in water, and its returning blood (17%) is oxygenated.

questions.question: From the diagram of structures in part of a cell membrane (options AQ, BR, CT, DV), which structure prevents large polar molecules from diffusing through the membrane?
questions.answer: B: R.
steps: R is the fatty acid tails, which form the hydrophobic core of the bilayer.
Large polar molecules cannot dissolve in this hydrophobic core, so they cannot diffuse through it.
Q is a phosphate head, T a glycoprotein and V a carrier protein, none of which acts as the barrier.

questions.question: From the membrane diagram (options AP, BS, CT, DU), which structure allows ions to diffuse through the membrane?
questions.answer: D: U.
steps: U is a protein that spans the whole membrane and forms a water-filled pore, so it is a channel protein.
Ions are charged, so they cannot cross the hydrophobic core and diffuse through channel proteins such as U.

questions.question: From the membrane diagram (options AP, BQ, CS, DU), which structure allows the membrane to be fluid?
questions.answer: C: S.
steps: S is a phospholipid molecule.
The phospholipids can move sideways past each other, which makes the membrane fluid.

questions.question: Which diagram shows the correct position of a cholesterol molecule in the membrane?
questions.answer: B.
steps: Cholesterol sits between the phospholipids, in line with the fatty acid tails, with its small polar -OH group next to the hydrophilic phosphate heads.

In B, the polar -OH end is at the heads and the hydrophobic rings lie among the tails; in A the -OH group faces the middle of the bilayer, in C the molecule lies flat in the middle of the bilayer, and in D the -OH group is in the middle of the bilayer, away from the heads.

questions.question: Describe the effect of temperature and cholesterol on membrane fluidity, shown in the graph.
questions.answer: Membrane fluidity increases with temperature in both cases; cholesterol makes fluidity change gradually with temperature, raising it at low temperature and lowering it at high temperature.
steps: Without cholesterol the fluidity is very low at low temperature, then rises steeply in the middle of the range, and levels off at high temperature.
With cholesterol the fluidity rises steadily (almost linearly) with temperature.
At low temperatures the membrane with cholesterol is more fluid than without, and at high temperatures (above the crossover point) it is less fluid than without cholesterol.
Both reach about the same fluidity at the top of the range, so cholesterol buffers the membrane against changes in temperature.

questions.question: Calculate the ratio of protein to lipid in membrane A from the table of composition of three membranes, giving the answer to 2 decimal places (as x : 1).
steps: Protein : lipid in membrane A = 49 : 43.
Divide by the lipid value: 49 / 43 = 1.14, so the ratio is 1.14 : 1.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the composition of the three membranes A, B and C in the table of protein, lipid and carbohydrate.
questions.answer: All three membranes contain protein, lipid and carbohydrate in different proportions: protein increases A < B < C, whereas lipid and carbohydrate decrease A > B > C, and C contains no carbohydrate.
steps: Similarities: all three contain protein and lipid, and in each membrane the protein percentage is larger than the lipid percentage; A and B are similar (49 and 54% protein, 43 and 42% lipid).
Difference: protein is 49% in A, 54% in B and 75% in C, so C has much more protein.
Difference: lipid is 43% in A, 42% in B and only 25% in C.
Difference: carbohydrate is 8% in A, 4% in B and 0% in C, so C has no glycoproteins or glycolipids.
